There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” they replied. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, when a person has crossed over the flood, what is it that he has crossed over? What is it that he has gone beyond? What is it that he has abandoned? What is it that he has fully understood? “Venerable sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One, guided by the Blessed One, and take recourse in the Blessed One. It would be good if the Blessed One himself would clarify the meaning of these words. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it. “Then listen, bhikkhus, and attend closely. I shall speak. “Yes, venerable sir,” the bhikkhus replied. The Blessed One said this: “When a person has crossed over the flood, bhikkhus, he has crossed over attachment; he has gone beyond clinging; he has abandoned craving; and he has fully understood ignorance. When a person has crossed over the flood, bhikkhus, he has crossed over attachment; he has gone beyond clinging; he has abandoned craving; and he has fully understood ignorance. Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We will cross over attachment; we will go beyond clinging; we will abandon craving; and we will fully understand ignorance. Thus, bhikkhus, should you train yourselves. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, those bhikkhus delighted in the Blessed One’s words. Thus have I heard. Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Then, when the night had advanced, a certain deity of surpassing beauty, illuminating the entire Jeta’s Grove, approached.
Having illuminated [the area], he approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he stood to one side.
Standing to one side, that deity said this to the Blessed One:
"How indeed, dear sir, did you cross the flood?"
“Friend, I have crossed the flood without a foothold and without effort.
“But how, dear sir, did you cross the flood without a foothold and without effort?
“Friend, whenever I would stand still, I would sink; whenever I would make an effort, I would be swept away. But when I neither stood still nor made an effort, I crossed over.”
"Friend, whenever I exerted myself, I would sink;
thus, friend, have I crossed the flood without a foothold and without exertion.
"After a long time, indeed, do I see you!"
The brahmin has attained final nibbāna—
without a foundation, without grasping,
having crossed over attachment to the world.
This is what that deity said.
The Teacher approved.
Then that deity [thought]:
“‘The Teacher has approved of me,’” he said, and having paid homage to the Blessed One and circumambulated him,
he vanished right there. *Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.2 (Naḷavagga)*
The Nimokkha Sutta.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Then, when the night had advanced, a certain deity of surpassing beauty, illuminating the entire Jeta’s Grove, approached.
Having illuminated [the area], he approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he stood to one side.
Standing to one side, that deity said this to the Blessed One:
"Do you know, dear sir, the liberation, the release, and the seclusion of beings?"
“I know, friend, the liberation, the release, and the seclusion of beings.
“But in what way, dear sir, do you know the liberation, the release, and the seclusion of beings?
“Through the total destruction of delight in existence (*nandībhava*):”
With the cessation and subsiding of perception and consciousness,
and the cessation and subsiding of feelings—
thus indeed, friend, do I know.
“Liberation, release, and seclusion for beings.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 1.3 (SN 1.3, SN 3, PTS [1st ed. SN i 2, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 4) 1. Naḷavagga (The Chapter on Reeds)
The Upanīyasutta.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Standing to one side, that deity recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:
“Life is being led away, its span is short;
for one led by old age, there are no refuges.
Seeing this danger in death, [one should practice].”
“One should perform meritorious deeds that bring happiness.
“Life is led away, its duration short;
for one led by old age, there are no refuges.”
"Perceiving this danger in death, one who seeks peace should abandon the bait of the world.
*Saṁyutta Nikāya 1.4* (SN 1.4, SN 4, PTS [1st ed. SN i 3, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 5)
1. The Chapter on Reeds:
The Discourse on the Acacia Tree.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Standing to one side, that deity recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:
“Time passes away, the nights fly by;
the qualities of youth are gradually abandoned.”
“Perceiving this danger in death, one should perform meritorious deeds that bring happiness.
Time passes; the nights hasten by.
The qualities of vitality are abandoned in succession;
seeing this danger in death,
one who seeks peace should abandon the bait of the world.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.5 (SN 1.5, SN 5, PTS [1st ed. SN i 3, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 5) 1. Naḷavagga Katichindasutta (The Discourse on Cutting a Few) At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, suppose a man were to cut a few blades of reed with a sharp knife; this would be a mere trifle compared to the amount of suffering that has been cut off by one who, for seven years, has abandoned the five lower fetters. “Bhikkhus, suppose a man were to cut a few blades of reed with a sharp knife; this would be a mere trifle compared to the amount of suffering that has been cut off by one who, for six years... five years... four years... three years... two years... one year... seven months... six months... five months... four months... three months... two months... one month... half a month... seven days... six days... five days... four days... three days... two days... one day... twelve hours... six hours... five hours... four hours... three hours... two hours... one hour... thirty minutes... fifteen minutes... ten minutes... five minutes... three minutes... two minutes... one minute... thirty seconds... fifteen seconds... ten seconds... five seconds... three seconds... two seconds... one second... half a second, has abandoned the five lower fetters. “Bhikkhus, suppose a man were to cut a few blades of reed with a sharp knife; this would be a mere trifle compared to the amount of suffering that has been cut off by one who, for the duration of a single breath-in and breath-out, has abandoned the five lower fetters.”
At Sāvatthī.
Standing to one side, that deity recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:
“How many should one cut off? How many should one abandon?”
How many should one cultivate further?
How many must a bhikkhu transcend to be called "one who has crossed the flood"?
“One should cut off five, abandon five,
and develop five further;
the bhikkhu who has transcended the five fetters— ”
“He is called one who has crossed the flood.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 1.6 (SN 1.6, SN 6, PTS [1st ed. SN i 3, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 6) 1. The Chapter on Reeds (Naḷavagga)
The Jāgara Sutta.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Standing to one side, that deity recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:
“How many who are awake are asleep?
How many among those asleep are awake?
By how many does one take up the dust?”
“By how many is one purified?
“Five who are awake among those who sleep,
and five who are asleep among those who are awake.”
“By five things one takes up passion; by five things one is purified. (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.7)
1. The Naḷa Chapter:
The Discourse on Not Penetrating.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Standing to one side, that deity recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:
“Those who have not fully penetrated the Dhamma Are led away by the doctrines of others.”
“They do not wake up from their slumber;
it is time for them to awaken.
“Those by whom the Dhammas have been well-penetrated...”
They are not led away by the doctrines of others;
those perfectly awakened ones, possessing right knowledge,
move with equanimity even amidst the uneven.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 1.8 (SN 1.8, SN 8, PTS [1st ed. SN i 4, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 7) 1. Naḷavagga Susammuṭṭhasutta – The Discourse on Being Well-Confused At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is well-confused about form, he is not one who dwells contemplating the body in the body; he is not one who dwells contemplating feelings in feelings; he is not one who dwells contemplating mind in the mind; he is not one who dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena. When a bhikkhu is well-confused about feeling … about perception … about volitional formations … about consciousness, he is not one who dwells contemplating the body in the body; he is not one who dwells contemplating feelings in feelings; he is not one who dwells contemplating mind in the mind; he is not one who dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena. But when a bhikkhu is not confused about form, he is one who dwells contemplating the body in the body; he is one who dwells contemplating feelings in feelings; he is one who dwells contemplating mind in the mind; he is one who dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena. When a bhikkhu is not confused about feeling … about perception … about volitional formations … about consciousness, he is one who dwells contemplating the body in the body; he is one who dwells contemplating feelings in feelings; he is one who dwells contemplating mind in the mind; he is one who dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” they replied. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is well-confused about form, he is not one who dwells contemplating the body in the body; he is not one who dwells contemplating feelings in feelings; he is not one who dwells contemplating mind in the mind; he is not one who dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena. When a bhikkhu is well-confused about feeling … about perception … about volitional formations … about consciousness, he is not one who dwells contemplating the body in the body; he is not one who dwells contemplating feelings in feelings; he is not one who dwells contemplating mind in the mind; he is not one who dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena. But when a bhikkhu is not confused about form, he is one who dwells contemplating the body in the body; he is one who dwells contemplating feelings in feelings; he is one who dwells contemplating mind in the mind; he is one who dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena. When a bhikkhu is not confused about feeling … about perception … about volitional formations … about consciousness, he is one who dwells contemplating the body in the body; he is one who dwells contemplating feelings in feelings; he is one who dwells contemplating mind in the mind; he is one who dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena. This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Fortunate One, the Teacher, further said this: “When one is confused about form, About feeling and perception, And about volitional formations and consciousness, One does not discern the noble Dhamma. But when one is not confused about form, About feeling and perception, And about volitional formations and consciousness, One discerns the noble Dhamma. When one has discerned the noble Dhamma, One becomes one who has seen the Dhamma; Having become one who has seen the Dhamma, One attains final Nibbāna in this very life.”
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Standing to one side, that deity recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:
“For those whose teachings are utterly forgotten...”
They are led away by the doctrines of others;
they sleep and do not awaken.
It is time for them to wake up.
“Those for whom the teachings are not forgotten,
who are not led astray by the doctrines of others—
they are the perfectly awakened ones, possessing right knowledge.”
“They wander among the uneven.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 1.9 (SN 1.9, SN 9, PTS [1st ed. SN i 4, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 8) 1. The Chapter on Reeds (Naḷavagga)
The Discourse on One Who Desires Honor.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Standing to one side, that deity recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:
“For one who desires honor, there is no self-control here;
for one who is unconcentrated, there is no silence.
Dwelling alone in the forest, yet being heedless—”
One would not cross to the further shore of the realm of death.
Having abandoned conceit, with a well-composed self,
pure-minded and entirely liberated from all [bonds];
Dwelling alone in the forest, being diligent, he shall cross to the further shore of the realm of Death.
*Saṁyutta Nikāya 1.10* (SN 1.10, SN 10, PTS [1st ed. SN i 5, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 9)
1. Naḷavagga Araññasutta.
Setting at Sāvatthī.
Standing to one side, that deity addressed the Blessed One in verse:
“For those who dwell in the forest,
peaceful and living the holy life;”
"For those who eat but one meal a day,
by what does their complexion become serene?
"They do not grieve over the past..."
They do not long for what has not yet come;
they subsist on the present,
and by that their complexion becomes serene.
Through longing for the future and grieving for the past,
by this the fools wither away.
“Like a green reed that has been cut down.
The first chapter, the Naḷa-vagga.
Its summary verse:
The flood that must be crossed,
those who have reached liberation and those who have cut the bonds— these pass away while others remain unawakened and unaware.
Susammuṭṭhā, Mānakāminā,
and Araññe as the tenth;
by this, the chapter is called.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.11 (SN 1.11, SN 11, PTS [1st ed. SN i 5, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 11) 2. Nandanavagga Nandanasutta Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, there are these five cords of sensual pleasure. What five? Forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust. Sounds cognizable by the ear... Odors cognizable by the nose... Flavors cognizable by the tongue... Tangibles cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust. These are the five cords of sensual pleasure. Now, bhikkhus, for a person who is not devoid of lust, desire, affection, thirst, passion, and craving for these five cords of sensual pleasure, there is delight; for one who delights, there is attachment; for one who is attached, there is bondage. Suppose, bhikkhus, there is a young man or a young woman, fond of ornaments, who has never before seen a royal tusker elephant, a well-bred one, a long-established royal lineage, possessed of the seven limbs. Then his father or mother would bring him to a royal tusker elephant, a well-bred one, a long-established royal lineage, possessed of the seven limbs, and say: ‘Child, this is a royal tusker elephant, a well-bred one, a long-established royal lineage, possessed of the seven limbs. Child, you should mount this royal tusker elephant and go wherever you wish. Then, having mounted the royal tusker elephant, he would go out from the city and enjoy himself on the back of the royal tusker elephant. While enjoying himself on the back of the royal tusker elephant, he would see a village pasture and think: ‘I am indeed mounted upon a royal tusker elephant, a well-bred one, a long-established royal lineage, possessed of the seven limbs. I am going wherever I wish, and I can even see a village pasture. He would become even more delighted and elated. Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Monks,” [the Blessed One said]. “Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One spoke as follows:
“Once upon a time, monks, a certain deity from the Tāvatiṃsa host, surrounded by a throng of nymphs in the Nandana Grove,
endowed and possessed of the fivefold divine cords of sensual pleasure while enjoying them, on that occasion spoke this verse:
‘They do not understand happiness;’”
Those who do not see Nandana,
the abode of the glorious gods of the thirty-three and of men.”
When this was said, bhikkhus, a certain deity replied to that deity in verse:
“O fool, you do not understand the word of the Arahants as it truly is.”
All conditioned phenomena are impermanent,
subject to the nature of arising and passing away;
having arisen, they cease.
“The subsiding of these is bliss.

The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Standing to one side, that deity recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:
One who has sons rejoices in his sons;
likewise, one who has cattle rejoices in his cattle.
A man’s delight comes from his acquisitions.
"For he does not rejoice who is free from acquisitions.
"One with sons sorrows because of his sons;
likewise, one with cattle sorrows because of his cattle."
“From acquisitions comes a man’s sorrow;
he who is without acquisitions does not grieve. (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.13)
2. The Chapter on Delight.
Discourse on the One Equal to One Who Has No Son.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Standing to one side, that deity recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:
“There is no love equal to that for a son;
there is no wealth equal to cattle.”
“There is no radiance equal to the sun;
there is no lake greater than the ocean.
“There is no love equal to self-love;”
There is no wealth equal to grain;
there is no radiance equal to wisdom;
indeed, rain is supreme among floods.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 1.14 (SN 1.14, SN 14, PTS [1st ed. SN i 6, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 13) 2. Nandanavagga Khattiyasutta “Monks, there are these four kinds of khattiyas. What four? The khattiya who is a khattiya by birth but not by conduct; the khattiya who is a khattiya by conduct but not by birth; the khattiya who is neither a khattiya by birth nor by conduct; and the khattiya who is a khattiya both by birth and by conduct. And how, monks, is one a khattiya by birth but not by conduct? Here, monks, someone is born into a clan of khattiyas, into a family of khattiyas, having been conceived through their union, born from their womb, and raised within them. But he does not practice the conduct of a khattiya. This, monks, is called a khattiya who is a khattiya by birth but not by conduct. And how, monks, is one a khattiya by conduct but not by birth? Here, monks, someone is born into a clan of commoners or a clan of merchants, having been conceived through their union, born from their womb, and raised within them. But he practices the conduct of a khattiya. This, monks, is called a khattiya who is a khattiya by conduct but not by birth. And how, monks, is one neither a khattiya by birth nor by conduct? Here, monks, someone is born into a clan of outcasts or a clan of hunters, having been conceived through their union, born from their womb, and raised within them. He does not practice the conduct of a khattiya. This, monks, is called a khattiya who is neither a khattiya by birth nor by conduct. And how, monks, is one a khattiya both by birth and by conduct? Here, monks, someone is born into a clan of khattiyas, into a family of khattiyas, having been conceived through their union, born from their womb, and raised within them. And he practices the conduct of a khattiya. This, monks, is called a khattiya who is a khattiya both by birth and by conduct. These, monks, are the four kinds of khattiyas.”
“The Khattiya is the best among bipeds,
the ox the best among quadrupeds;
the maiden is the best among wives.”
“And he who is the first-born among sons.
“The Fully Awakened One is the best of bipeds;
the well-bred horse is the best of quadrupeds.”
“Obedience is the best among wives, and that which is obedient is the best among sons.
— Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.15 (SN 1.15, SN 15, PTS [1st ed. SN i 7, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 13)
2. The Chapter on Delight: The Discourse on the Mind’s Tendency “At the time when midday has arrived, [the mind] inclines toward the objects of sensual pleasure.”
When the birds have settled down,
the great forest seems to whisper;
that fear appears to me."
When the time of midday had arrived and the birds were settled down,
the great forest was as if hushed in silence.
"That delight appears to me," he said.
*Saṁyutta Nikāya* 1.16 (SN 1.16, SN 16, PTS [1st ed. SN i 7, PTS [2nd ed.
SN i 14) 2. Nandanavagga
The Discourse on Drowsiness and Sloth: “Drowsiness, sloth, yawning,
discontent, and drowsiness from overeating;”
“By this, the Noble Path does not shine forth here for living beings. [And:
“Sleep, drowsiness, and yawning...”
Having dispelled discontent and the drowsiness of overeating through energy,
the Noble Path is purified.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 1.17 (SN 1.17, SN 17, PTS [1st ed. SN i 7, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 15) 2. Nandanavagga Dukkarasutta (The Discourse on What is Difficult to Do) “Monks, it is difficult to do; it is very difficult to do. And what, monks, is difficult to do? It is difficult to do to dwell with a mind free from enmity and ill will, vast, exalted, and measureless, toward all beings. This, monks, is difficult to do. It is difficult to do to dwell with a mind free from enmity and ill will, vast, exalted, and measureless, toward the entire world. This, monks, is difficult to do. It is difficult to do to dwell with a mind free from enmity and ill will, vast, exalted, and measureless, toward the whole world, including the devas, Māras, and Brahmās, and the world with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans. This, monks, is difficult to do.”
“Difficult to do and difficult to endure is the state of a recluse for one who is incompetent;
therein there are many obstructions.”
“Wherein the fool falters.
“How long could one practice the life of a recluse if one does not restrain the mind?”
At every step he would falter,
being subject to the power of his own intentions.
Like a tortoise with its limbs withdrawn into its own shell...
A bhikkhu who has stilled mental thoughts,
independent, not harming others,
and fully extinguished, would never revile anyone.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.18 (SN 1.18, SN 18, PTS [1st ed. SN i 7, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 16) 2. Nandanavagga Hirīsutta “Monks, there are these two kinds of shamelessness. What two? Shamelessness regarding oneself and shamelessness regarding others. These, monks, are the two kinds of shamelessness. “Monks, there are these two kinds of moral dread. What two? Moral dread regarding oneself and moral dread regarding others. These, monks, are the two kinds of moral dread. “Monks, there are these two kinds of shame. What two? Shame regarding oneself and shame regarding others. These, monks, are the two kinds of shame. “Monks, there are these two kinds of moral dread. What two? Moral dread regarding oneself and moral dread regarding others. These, monks, are the two kinds of moral dread. “Monks, for one who possesses these two qualities—shame regarding oneself and moral dread regarding others—I do not see even a single place where they might go that would not lead to their welfare and happiness. But for one who possesses these two qualities—shamelessness regarding oneself and shamelessness regarding others—I do not see even a single place where they might go that would not lead to their harm and suffering. “Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We shall possess shame regarding ourselves and moral dread regarding others. It is in this way, monks, that you should train yourselves.”
“There is found in this world some man who is restrained by a sense of shame,
who awakens from blame.”
“Like a noble horse [shaking off] the whip.
“Those who always conduct themselves with mindfulness, restrained by the slender cord of moral shame;”
"Having reached the end of suffering, they wander as recluses on uneven ground.
— Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.19 (SN 1.19, SN 19, PTS [1st ed. SN i 8, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 17)
2. Nandanavagga Kuṭikāsutta “I hope you have no small huts?”
I hope you have no family nest;
I hope there are no creeping vines;
I hope you are released from all bonds.
“Truly, for me there is no hut;
truly, there is no nest;
truly, there are no cobwebs.”
“Truly, I am released from bondage.
“What do I call a hut?
What do I call a nest for you?”
"What do I call 'kinsman,' and what do I call 'bondage'?
"You call one's mother a 'hovel'."
"You call the wife a bird's nest;
you call the children the lineage;
you call craving my bond."
“Excellent that you have no hut;
excellent that you have no nest;
excellent that you have no canopy.”
“Well done, you are liberated from bondage.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 1.20 (SN 1.20, SN 20, PTS [1st ed. SN i 8, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 18) 2.
Nandanavagga (The Chapter on Delight)
The Samiddhi Sutta:
Thus have I heard—
on one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Tapodā Park.
Then, as the night was drawing to a close, the Venerable Samiddhi rose and went to the hot springs to bathe his limbs.
Having bathed his limbs in the hot springs and emerged, he stood there wearing a single robe, drying his limbs.
Then, at the end of the night, a certain deity of surpassing beauty approached the entire extent of the hot springs.
Having illuminated [the area], he approached the Venerable Samiddhi; having approached, standing in the air, he addressed the Venerable Samiddhi with a verse:
“Without eating, you wander for alms, O bhikkhu.”
For you do not beg after having eaten; having eaten, O bhikkhu,
go forth begging, lest the time pass you by.
“I do not know the time;
the time is hidden and not seen.
Therefore, I wander for alms without having eaten.”
“Let not time pass me by!
Then that deity, having established herself upon the earth, said this to the Venerable Samiddhi:
“Bhikkhu, you are young, having gone forth while still a youth with black hair, endowed with the splendor of youth, in the prime of life, and one who has not yet sported with sensual pleasures.”
“Enjoy, bhikkhu, human sensual pleasures;
do not abandon what is directly visible and run after what is delayed.
“I do not, friend, abandon what is directly visible to run after what is delayed.”
"Friend, having set aside what is temporal, I pursue what is directly visible.
For the Blessed One has said, friend, that sensual pleasures are temporal, fraught with much suffering and much despair; the danger here is greater.
But this Dhamma is directly visible, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, to be realized by the wise for themselves."
“And how, bhikkhu, have sensual pleasures been described by the Blessed One as temporal, fraught with much suffering and much despair, wherein the danger is greater?
And how is this Dhamma directly visible, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, to be personally realized by the wise?
“I am new, friend, recently gone forth, having only just come to this Dhamma and Vinaya.”
I am not able to explain this to you in detail.
That Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One, is staying at Rājagaha in the Tapodārāma.
Go to that Blessed One and ask him about this matter.
“Just as the Blessed One explains it to you, so should you remember it.
“But, bhikkhu, it is not easy for us to approach that Blessed One, for he is surrounded by other deities of great influence.
However, bhikkhu, if you were to approach that Blessed One and ask him about this matter, we too would come to hear the Dhamma.”
“Yes, friend,” the Venerable Samiddhi replied to that deity.
He then approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Samiddhi said this to the Blessed One:
“Here, Bhante, rising at the time of dawn during the night, I went to the Tapodā to bathe my limbs.
Having bathed my limbs in the Tapodā and come out, I stood there wearing a single robe, drying my limbs.

Then, Bhante, a certain deity, at the end of the night, having approached with surpassing beauty and illuminating the entire Tapodā, came to where I was; having approached and standing in the air, she addressed me with this verse:”
“Without having eaten, you beg, O bhikkhu;
for you do not beg after having eaten.
Having eaten, bhikkhu, you should beg.”
‘Let not time pass you by.
When this was said, Bhante, I replied to that deity with a verse:
‘I do not know the time.’”
"The opportune time is not seen;
therefore, I shall go for alms without eating,
lest time should overtake me."
Then, venerable sir, that deity, having established herself upon the earth, said this to me:
"You are young, bhikkhu, having gone forth while still a youth with black hair, endowed with the blessing of youth, in the prime of life, and you have not yet enjoyed sensual pleasures.
Enjoy, bhikkhu, human sensual pleasures!"
"Do not abandon what is directly visible and pursue what belongs to the future.
When this was said, venerable sir, I replied to that deity:
"Friend, I do not abandon what is directly visible to pursue what belongs to the future."
"Friends, having abandoned what is temporal, I pursue what is visible in this very life.
For the Blessed One has said that sensual pleasures are temporal, fraught with much suffering and much despair, and the danger therein is greater.
This Dhamma, however, is visible in this very life, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, and to be personally realized by the wise."
When this was said, venerable sir, that deity said this to me:
“And how, bhikkhu, have sensual pleasures been described by the Blessed One as bringing much suffering and much despair, with more danger still in them?
And how is this Dhamma directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally realized by the wise?”
When this was said, venerable sir, I replied to that deity:
“I am indeed new, friend, recently gone forth, having only just come to this Dhamma and Discipline; I am not able to explain it in detail.
That Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One, is staying at Rājagaha in the Tapodā Monastery.”
“Having approached that Blessed One, ask him about this matter.
Just as the Blessed One explains it to you, so should you remember it.
When this was said, Bhante, that deity spoke to me thus:
“Monk, it is not easy for us to approach that Blessed One, as he is surrounded by other deities of great influence.
If you, monk, were to approach that Blessed One and ask about this matter, we too would come to hear the Dhamma.
“Venerable sir, if that deity’s words are true, then that deity is right here, not far away.”
When this was said, that deity spoke thus to the Venerable Samiddhi:
“Ask, monk! Ask, monk! I have arrived for that purpose.
Then the Blessed One addressed that deity with verses:
“Beings perceive what can be expressed,
and they are established upon what can be expressed;
not having fully understood what can be expressed, [they suffer].”
They enter the snare of death.
Having fully understood what can be expressed,
one does not conceive of an expresser.
"For that which he does not have, by which one might speak of him, that he has not.
If you know it, tell me, O Yakkha."
“Venerable sir, I do not understand in detail the meaning of this statement spoken in brief by the Blessed One.
It would be well, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would speak to me in such a way that I might understand in detail the meaning of this statement spoken in brief by the Blessed One.
“Is he equal, superior, or indeed inferior?”
He who conceives [notions] would dispute because of that;
but for one who is unshakable regarding the three kinds of classification,
the thought "I am equal" or "I am superior" does not occur.
“If you understand, then speak, O Yakkha.
“Venerable sir, even for this which has been spoken in brief by the Blessed One, I do not understand the meaning in detail.
It would be well, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would explain it in such a way that I might understand in detail the meaning of what was spoken in brief by the Blessed One.”
“He has abandoned conceit and found no grounds for pride;
he has cut off craving here for name-and-form.
With his fetters severed, free from distress, and devoid of longing—”
Searching for him, they did not find him—
neither gods nor humans, here or in the world beyond,
nor in all the celestial abodes.
“If you understand, tell me, O yakkha.
“Venerable sir, I understand the detailed meaning of this brief statement by the Blessed One thus:
‘One should not do evil with speech or with the mind...’”
Having abandoned all sensual desires in the entire world with the body, being mindful and clearly comprehending,
one should not pursue suffering which leads to what is unbeneficial.
The second chapter, the Nandanavagga.
Its summary verse (uddāna) is:
Nandanā, and also Nandati.
And one who has no son; a kshatriya seeking [status], and one who is sleepless and slothful—
these find it difficult [to practice].
Modesty is the hut;
the tenth is said to be Samiddhi.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 1.21 (SN 1.21, SN 21, PTS [1st ed. SN i 13, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 27).
3. The Section on Power (Sattivagga). The Discourse on Power (Sattisutta).
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Standing to one side, that deity recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:
“As if struck by a spear,
as if my head were on fire;”
“For the abandoning of sensual lust,
let the mindful bhikkhu wander forth.
Like one struck by a spear, he wanders.
As if his head were on fire,
a bhikkhu should wander mindfully for the sake of abandoning the view of a personal body.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 1.22 (SN 1.22, SN 22, PTS [1st ed. SN i 13, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 27) 3. Sattivagga Phusatisutta “Bhikkhus, when one touches with the body a form that is pleasant, desirable, agreeable, charming, connected with sensual pleasure, and provocative of lust, and one does not feel desire for it, then that form is not bondage for that person; rather, it is that person who is bound by that form. When one touches with the body a form that is painful, undesirable, disagreeable, uncharming, connected with suffering, and provocative of grief, and one feels aversion toward it, then that form is not bondage for that person; rather, it is that person who is bound by that form. When one touches with the body a form that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant, and one dwells with a mind obsessed by equanimity, accompanied by ignorance, then that form is not bondage for that person; rather, it is that person who is bound by that form. Bhikkhus, when one touches with the body a form that is pleasant, desirable, agreeable, charming, connected with sensual pleasure, and provocative of lust, and one does not feel desire for it, then that form is bondage for that person. When one touches with the body a form that is painful, undesirable, disagreeable, uncharming, connected with suffering, and provocative of grief, and one feels aversion toward it, then that form is bondage for that person. When one touches with the body a form that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant, and one dwells with a mind obsessed by equanimity, accompanied by ignorance, then that form is bondage for that person. Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We shall not touch with the body a form that is pleasant, desirable, agreeable, charming, connected with sensual pleasure, and provocative of lust, and we shall not feel desire for it. ‘We shall not touch with the body a form that is painful, undesirable, disagreeable, uncharming, connected with suffering, and provocative of grief, and we shall not feel aversion toward it. ‘We shall not touch with the body a form that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant, and we shall not dwell with a mind obsessed by equanimity, accompanied by ignorance. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that you should train yourselves.”
"It does not touch one who does not touch,
but it touches one who touches;
therefore, it touches the one who touches."
"Against one who is not ill-disposed, who harbors no malice. "He who bears malice toward a man who is not ill-disposed,
toward a pure person free from blemish..."
“Evil follows that fool,
just as fine dust thrown against the wind. (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.23)
3. The Section on Powers (Sattivagga) The Tangled Hair Discourse (Jaṭāsutta): “Tangled within, tangled without, ... [the mind] is entangled in the world.”
People are entangled in a tangle;
O Gotama, I ask you this:
who can disentangle this tangle?
“Established in virtue, a wise man,
developing his mind and wisdom,
a bhikkhu who is ardent and discerning— ”
Therefore, one should unravel this tangle:
for those by whom lust, hatred,
and ignorance have been faded away.
The Arahants whose taints are destroyed—
their tangles are disentangled—
wherein both name-and-form [cease].
Ceases without remainder;
there, this tangle of resentment and perception of form is cut off.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 1.24 (SN 1.24, SN 24, PTS [1st ed. SN i 14, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 29) 3. Sattivagga Manonivāraṇasutta: The Discourse on the Warding Off of the Mind “Bhikkhus, when the mind is not warded off, unwholesome states increase; when the mind is warded off, unwholesome states do not increase. “And how, bhikkhus, is the mind not warded off so that unwholesome states increase? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells with his mind unprotected by mindfulness regarding the body, and he does not understand as it really is the arising and passing away of feelings. This is how the mind is not warded off so that unwholesome states increase. “And how, bhikkhus, is the mind warded off so that unwholesome states do not increase? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells with his mind protected by mindfulness regarding the body, and he understands as it really is the arising and passing away of feelings. This is how the mind is warded off so that unwholesome states do not increase.”
“From whatever direction one restrains the mind,
from that very direction suffering does not come to it; therefore,
one should restrain the mind from all directions.”
“He is liberated from suffering on every side.
“One should not restrain the mind from everything,
nor should one allow the mind to come under restraint.”
“From whatever direction evil comes, from that very direction one should restrain the mind.
— *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 1.25 (SN 1.25, SN 25, PTS [1st ed. SN i 14; PTS [2nd ed. SN i 30)
3. The Section on Powers (Sattivagga) The Discourse on the Worthy One (Arahantasutta) “Whatever bhikkhu is a worthy one (arahant), one who has accomplished what was to be done...”
“One whose taints are destroyed, who bears his final body—
such a one might say, ‘I speak,’ and he might also say, ‘They speak of me.’”
“Whatever monk is an arahant, accomplished,
whose taints are exhausted, and who bears his final body—
if he were to say, ‘I am,’ I would say that he speaks thus.”
"He might even say, 'They are speaking of me'; for,
being skilled in understanding the conventional designations used in the world,
he would employ them as mere worldly expressions."
“That bhikkhu who is an arahant, accomplished,
whose taints are destroyed, who bears his final body—
would that bhikkhu, having approached, give way to conceit?”
“He might say, ‘I speak,’ and he might also say, ‘They speak of me.
For one who has abandoned conceit, there are no fetters.”
All the fetters of conceit have been shaken off by him;
that wise one has transcended all notions of "I am," yet he might still say, "I speak."
"He might even say, 'They speak of me,' having understood that it is merely a conventional designation in the world;
he would employ such speech as a mere worldly convention."

Saṁyutta Nikāya 1.26 (SN 1.26, SN 26, PTS [1st ed. SN i 15, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 32) 3. Sattivagga Pajjotasutta (The Lamp) Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, suppose there were a lamp burning in a house with closed doors. Its light would not shine out through the windows, nor through the door-slits, nor through the keyholes. Why is that? Because it is obstructed by the walls of the house. In the same way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who is full of lust, hatred, and delusion—whose mind is obsessed by lust, hatred, and delusion—does not understand as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; he does not understand as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he does not understand as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he does not understand as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. Why is that? Because he is obstructed by lust, hatred, and delusion. “Bhikkhus, suppose there were a lamp burning in a house with open doors. Its light would shine out through the windows, through the door-slits, and through the keyholes. Why is that? Because it is unobstructed by the walls of the house. In the same way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who is free from lust, hatred, and delusion—whose mind is not obsessed by lust, hatred, and delusion—understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. Why is that? Because he is unobstructed by lust, hatred, and delusion. This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Fortunate One, the Teacher, further said this: “The lamp of the Tathāgata shines forth, Dispelling the darkness of ignorance. It dispels all darkness, The lamp of the Buddha shines forth.”
“How many lights are there in the world by which the world is illuminated? Having approached,
I ask the Blessed One.”
“How shall we know you?
“There are four lamps in the world;
a fifth is not found here.”
The sun shines by day,
the moon radiates by night;
but fire [shines] both by day and by night.
He shines here and there; the Perfectly Enlightened One, the best of those who radiate heat—
this is his unsurpassed light.”

Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.27 (SN 1.27, SN 27, PTS [1st ed. SN i 15, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 33) 3. Sattivagga Sarasutta “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is like a shallow pool with a clear bottom, where one can see the shells, pebbles, and gravel, and where fish move about; the person who is like a deep pool with a clear bottom, where one cannot see the shells, pebbles, and gravel, nor where fish move about; the person who is like a deep pool with a turbid bottom, where one cannot see the shells, pebbles, and gravel, nor where fish move about; and the person who is like a deep pool with a turbid bottom, where one cannot see the shells, pebbles, and gravel, nor where fish move about, yet which is cool, sweet, and pure. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
“From where do the streams turn back?
Where does the cycle no longer revolve?
Where indeed do name-and-form cease?”
“Where water and earth, fire and wind find no footing, there everything ceases without remainder.”
From this, the currents turn back;
here the round does not proceed;
here name-and-form [cease].
“...it ceases without remainder.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 1.28 (SN 1.28, SN 28, PTS [1st ed. SN i 15, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 33) 3. Sattivagga (The Chapter on Arrows)
The Discourse on Great Wealth: “Those with great wealth and great enjoyments,
even kshatriyas possessing kingdoms;”
They greedily covet one another,
unadorned by sensual pleasures;
while they are thus striving for their own ends,
Among those who follow the stream of existence,
who have abandoned craving,
and who are free from anxiety in this world?
“Having left the home life and gone forth,
having abandoned son, cattle, and what is dear,
having abandoned both lust and hatred, [they dwell in peace].”
Having dispelled ignorance,
those Arhats whose taints are destroyed are free from longing for the world.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.29 (SN 1.29, SN 29, PTS [1st ed. SN i 16, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 35) 3. Sattivagga Catucakkasutta (The Discourse on the Four-Wheeled Chariot) "Bhikkhus, there are these four wheels that, when present, bring about the attainment of greatness for a wheel-turning monarch, a righteous king who rules by the Dhamma. What four? First, bhikkhus, a wheel-turning monarch, a righteous king who rules by the Dhamma, possesses a noble birth. This is the first wheel that, when present, brings about the attainment of greatness for a wheel-turning monarch, a righteous king who rules by the Dhamma. Second, bhikkhus, a wheel-turning monarch, a righteous king who rules by the Dhamma, possesses great wealth and property. This is the second wheel...
