Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We will give the Dhamma as much as we are able. It is in such a way that you should train yourselves.”
“What does one give to become strong?
What does one give to become beautiful?
What does one give to become happy?”
Who is the giver of sight?
And who is the giver of everything? Tell me that when you are asked.”
“One who gives food becomes strong;
one who gives clothing becomes beautiful;
one who gives a vehicle becomes happy.”
He is a giver of lamps and a giver of eyes;
he is indeed a giver of everything who gives a dwelling place.
“And he is a giver of the Deathless who instructs in the Dhamma. (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.43)
5. Ādittavagga.
Annasutta:
“They delight indeed in food;”
"Both gods and humans—
what indeed is that yakkha who does not delight in food?"
“Whatever food they give with faith,
with a mind full of serene confidence,
that very food attends upon them.”
In this world and in the next.
Therefore, having overcome stinginess,
one who has conquered impurity should give a gift.
“Meritorious deeds are the foundation for living beings in the world beyond.
*Saṁyutta Nikāya 1.44* (SN 1.44, SN 44, PTS [1st ed. SN i 32, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 68)
5. Ādittavagga Ekamūlasutta “One root, two turnings, ... [text continues] ...”
The seer crossed the Timala with its five stretches,
the ocean with its twelve whirlpools,
and the underworld.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.45 (SN 1.45, SN 45, PTS [1st ed. SN i 33, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 68) 5. Ādittavagga: Anoma Sutta Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Bhante, it is wonderful, Bhante, it is marvelous how the Blessed One has taught the Dhamma so thoroughly that a noble disciple who possesses this Dhamma would have no further need for another teacher. “It is so, Ānanda, it is so! It is wonderful, Ānanda, it is marvelous how I have taught the Dhamma so thoroughly that a noble disciple who possesses this Dhamma would have no further need for another teacher. For what reason? Because, Ānanda, a noble disciple who possesses this Dhamma understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. And what, Ānanda, is suffering? Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, illness is suffering, death is suffering; sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are suffering; association with the disliked is suffering, separation from the liked is suffering, not getting what one wishes for is suffering—in short, the five aggregates subject to clinging are suffering. This, Ānanda, is called suffering. And what, Ānanda, is the origin of suffering? It is craving, which brings renewal of being, is accompanied by delight and lust, and delights in this and that; that is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. This, Ānanda, is called the origin of suffering. And what, Ānanda, is the cessation of suffering? It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving, the relinquishing of it, the abandoning of it, the liberation from it, and the non-attachment to it. This, Ānanda, is called the cessation of suffering. And what, Ānanda, is the way leading to the cessation of suffering? It is simply this Noble Eightfold Path; that is, right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This, Ānanda, is called the way leading to the cessation of suffering. Because, Ānanda, a noble disciple who possesses this Dhamma understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’ ... ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering,’ therefore, Ānanda, a noble disciple who possesses this Dhamma would have no further need for another teacher.”
“Behold him of wondrous name, who perceives the subtle meaning,
the giver of wisdom, unattached to the abode of sensual desires—
him, the all-knowing one of great intelligence.”
“The Great Seer walking upon the noble path.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 1.46 (SN 1.46, SN 46, PTS [1st ed. SN i 33, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 69) 5. Ādittavagga (The Chapter on the Burning)
The Discourse on the Finger-Snap:
“Resounding with the clapping of finger-snaps,
frequented by hosts of piśācas;”
“The end of the forest is called Mohana;
how will the journey proceed?
“That path is indeed called Uju (the Straight).”
That direction is named Fearless;
the chariot is named Unrattling,
yoked with wheels of Dhamma.
Moral shame is its support,
mindfulness its protection;
I call the Dhamma the charioteer.
Preceded by right view—
whosoever, whether woman or man, possesses such a vehicle as this;
Truly, by means of this vehicle, he is indeed close to Nibbāna.
—Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.47 (SN 1.47, SN 47, PTS [1st ed. SN i 33; PTS [2nd ed. SN i 70)
5. Ādittavagga Vanaropasutta “Of whom,
both by day and by night, [is there no remorse]?”
Merit always increases for them.
Who are the people established in the Dhamma, endowed with virtue, who go to heaven?
“Those people who plant orchards and forests, those who build bridges,
and who provide public parks and wells— ”
For those who give a dwelling place,
their merit constantly increases, both by day and by night.
“Those people who are established in the Dhamma and perfected in virtue go to heaven.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 1.48 (SN 1.48, SN 48, PTS [1st ed. SN i 33, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 71)
5. Ādittavagga, Jetavanasutta:
“For this Jeta’s Grove—”
Frequented by the assembly of seers,
inhabited by the King of Dharma,
it generates joy within me.
Kamma, knowledge, and the Dhamma,
along with virtue as the supreme way of life—
by these mortals are purified.
Neither by lineage nor by wealth.
Therefore, a wise person,
clearly seeing his own welfare, [should practice virtue].
Investigate the Dhamma with systematic attention;
in this way one is purified therein.
Sāriputta is indeed supreme in wisdom.
"By virtue and by peace;
even a bhikkhu who has gone to the further shore could at most be no more than this."

Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.49 (SN 1.49, SN 49, PTS [1st ed. SN i 34, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 72) 5. Ādittavagga Maccharisutta (The Discourse on the Miserly One) "Bhikkhus, there are these five kinds of miserliness. What five? Miserliness regarding dwellings, miserliness regarding families, miserliness regarding gains, miserliness regarding praise, and miserliness regarding the Dhamma. These, bhikkhus, are the five kinds of miserliness."
“Those who are miserly in this world,
stingy, and abusive toward others as they give;”
People who create obstacles—
what is their ripening,
and what is their state in the future life?
“Having come to question the Blessed One,
how shall we understand that?
“Those who are miserly in this world...”
These people are miserly and abusive;
they create obstacles for others who are giving.
They are reborn in hell, in the animal realm,
or in the world of Yama;
even if they should come to human existence, [they are still afflicted].
Poverty arises in the family.
Where even food, pleasure, and play are obtained only with great difficulty;
Fools revile others,
yet they do not gain even that [retribution] from them;
the ripening of this occurs in this very life.
"And in the future life, an evil destination.
"Thus we understand this;
we ask another question, Gotama:"
Having obtained this human state,
being generous and free from stinginess,
they have faith in the Buddha and in the Dhamma.
And having intense reverence for the Saṅgha:
what will be their ripening,
and what will be their future state?
“Having come to question the Blessed One,
how shall we understand that?
“Those who have here attained the human state...”
Generous and free from stinginess,
they have clear confidence in the Buddha and the Dhamma,
and possess profound reverence for the Saṅgha.
These heavens shine forth where they have been reborn;
should they come back to the human state, [they will be born into noble families].
Born into a wealthy and noble family,
where alms-food, pleasure, and sport are obtained without difficulty— even in the land of Coḷa.
One who rejoices as if possessing mastery over enjoyments that belong to others experiences the ripening of this very fruit in the present life.
"And a happy destination in the life to come.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 1.50 (SN 1.50, SN 50, PTS [1st ed. SN i 35, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 75) 5. The Chapter on the Burning (Ādittavagga)
The Discourse to Ghaṭīkāra:
“Seven bhikkhus have been reborn in the Aviha heaven, liberated.”
"With lust and hatred utterly destroyed,
they have crossed over attachment to the world.
"And who are those who have crossed the mire?"
The realm of Death is so difficult to cross;
who, having abandoned the human body,
have transcended the celestial yoke?
“Upaka and Palagaṇḍa,
Pukkusāti— those three;
Bhaddiya and Khaṇḍadeva.”
Bāhuraggi and Siṅgiyo—
having abandoned their human bodies,
they have transcended to divine union.
“You speak rightly of those who have abandoned Mara’s snare;
having understood whose Dhamma, do you praise them?”
“...severed the bond of existence.
“None other than the Blessed One,
none other than your teaching;”
Having understood those teachings of yours,
they have severed the bond of existence,
wherein both name-and-form—
It ceases without remainder;
having understood that Dhamma here,
they have severed the bond of existence.
“You speak words that are profound,
difficult to discern and very hard to understand;
having understood whose Dhamma do you speak thus?”
“You speak such words! [He replied:
“In the past, I was a potter, a maker of jars in Vekaḷiṅga.”
I was a supporter of my mother and father,
a lay follower of Kassapa,
abstaining from sexual intercourse.
A celibate practitioner, free from worldly desires,
he was once a fellow villager of yours,
and he was once your friend in the past.
Thus do I understand these seven monks who are liberated,
in whom lust and hatred are utterly destroyed.
“Having crossed over attachment to the world.
“It was just so at that time,
Bhaggava, exactly as you have spoken.”
In the past, in Vekaḷiṅga, there was a potter, a maker of jars;
he was one who supported his mother and father.
A lay follower of Kassapa,
abstaining from sexual intercourse,
living a life of celibacy, free from worldly desires.
“He was my fellow villager;
he was my friend in the past.
“So it is with these ancient [beings].”
There was a meeting of companions—
of both those who had developed themselves and who bore their final bodies.
The fifth chapter, the Fire Chapter.
Its summary verse:
"On fire, what does it give? Food..."
Having uprooted this single root,
one fashions a water-pot out of the forest of the gods through stinginess.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 1.51 (SN 1.51, SN 51, PTS [1st ed. SN i 36, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 79) 6. Jarāvagga: Jarāsutta (The Discourse on Aging) “Bhikkhus, aging is suffering; illness is suffering; death is suffering. To one who has not abandoned lust for these things, who has not removed desire for them, who has not overcome craving for them, there is no escape from birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. This is called the Noble Truth of Suffering. “Bhikkhus, what is the origin of this suffering? It is that craving which gives rise to renewed existence, bound up with delight and lust, finding delight here and there—that is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. This is called the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering. “Bhikkhus, what is the cessation of this suffering? It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that same craving, the giving up and relinquishing of it, freedom from it, and non-reliance upon it. This is called the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering. “Bhikkhus, what is the way leading to the cessation of this suffering? It is simply this Noble Eightfold Path; that is, right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This is called the Noble Truth of the Way Leading to the Cessation of Suffering.”
“What is good as long as one lives?
What is good when well-established?
What is the jewel among men?”
"What is difficult for thieves to steal?
"Virtue is good until old age;
faith is good when firmly established."
Wisdom is the jewel of human beings;
merit is difficult for thieves to steal.
6. Jarāvagga Ajarasāsutta “What is it that is good because of freedom from decay?”
What is well-established?
What is the jewel among men?
And what is that which cannot be stolen by thieves?
“Virtue is good through its agelessness;
faith is good when firmly established;
wisdom is the jewel of human beings.”
“Merit is not to be stolen by thieves.
— *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 1.53 (SN 1.53, SN 53, PTS [1st ed. SN i 37; PTS [2nd ed. SN i 80) 6. Jarāvagga (The Chapter on Aging)
Mittasutta:
“What is a friend for one traveling abroad?
What is a friend in one’s own home?”
“What is a friend for one who has acquired wealth?
What is a friend for the future life?
“A caravan is a friend for one traveling abroad.”
A mother is a friend in one's own home;
a companion is a friend when one is in need,
a friend again and again.
“Meritorious deeds well performed—
this is one’s friend in the life to come. (Saṁyutta Nikāya 1.54)
6. The Chapter on Aging:
The Discourse on the Foundation “What is the foundation for human beings?”
Who here is the supreme friend?
What beings do those living creatures who depend upon the earth subsist upon?
“Sons are the foundation for humans,
and a wife is the supreme companion;
beings subsist upon the rain.”
“Those living beings who are established upon the earth.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 1.55 (SN 1.55, SN 55, PTS [1st ed. SN i 37, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 82) 6. The Chapter on Old Age (*Jarāvagga*)
The First Discourse on Begetting:
“What is it that begets a person? What is it that runs about for him?”
"What brings one into the cycle of existence? What is its greatest fear?
"Craving gives birth to a person."
His mind runs wild;
the being enters the cycle of existence,
for suffering is his great terror.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.56 (SN 1.56, SN 56, PTS [1st ed. SN i 37, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 82) 6. Jarāvagga Dutiyajanasutta (The Second Discourse on People) Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is bound by both ends and fettered in the middle; the person who is bound by both ends and freed in the middle; the person who is freed from both ends and fettered in the middle; and the person who is freed from both ends and freed in the middle. And how, bhikkhus, is a person bound by both ends and fettered in the middle? Here, someone is addicted to sensual pleasures in the past and is also addicted to sensual pleasures in the present. This is called a person bound by both ends and fettered in the middle. And how, bhikkhus, is a person bound by both ends and freed in the middle? Here, someone was addicted to sensual pleasures in the past but is not addicted to sensual pleasures in the present. This is called a person bound by both ends and freed in the middle. And how, bhikkhus, is a person freed from both ends and fettered in the middle? Here, someone is not addicted to sensual pleasures in the past but is addicted to sensual pleasures in the present. This is called a person freed from both ends and fettered in the middle. And how, bhikkhus, is a person freed from both ends and freed in the middle? Here, someone is not addicted to sensual pleasures in the past and is also not addicted to sensual pleasures in the present. This is called a person freed from both ends and freed in the middle. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Fortunate One, the Teacher, further said this: “The person bound by both ends, Fettered in the middle, Is swept away by the flood, Carried along by the current. But the person who has severed the bonds, Who has cut off all ties, Having abandoned the realm of death, Does not come back again to birth.”
“What gives birth to a person?
What runs about for him?
What undergoes the cycle of rebirth?”
“From what is one not liberated?
“Craving gives birth to the person;
his mind runs hither and thither.”
“The being undergoes saṃsāra;
he is not released from suffering.
— Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.57 (SN 1.57, SN 57, PTS [1st ed. SN i 38, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 83)
6. Jarāvagga Tatiyajanasutta “What gives birth to a person? What is it that makes one grow old?”
What runs away from him?
What undergoes the cycle of existence?
And what is his ultimate destination?”
“Craving gives birth to a person;
his mind runs hither and thither;
thus a being undergoes the cycle of existence.”
“Kamma is his destination.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 1.58 (SN 1.58, SN 58, PTS [1st ed. SN i 38, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 83) 6. Jarāvagga (The Chapter on Aging)
Uppathasutta:
“What is declared to be the wrong path?
What is that which exhausts the night and day?”
“What is the stain of the holy life?
What is the bath without water?
“Lust is declared to be the wrong path.”
Time is the wasting away of nights and days;
woman is the stain of the holy life,
wherein this generation becomes entangled.
"Austerity and the holy life—this is the bath that uses no water.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.59* (SN 1.59, SN 59, PTS [1st ed. SN i 38; PTS [2nd ed. SN i 84)
6. Jarāvagga, Second Discourse:
“What, indeed, is the companion of a person?”
By what is one governed?
By what does a mortal delight,
and by what is one liberated from all suffering?
“Faith is a person’s companion;
wisdom guides them.
A mortal who delights in Nibbāna—”
“One is liberated from all suffering.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 1.60 (SN 1.60, SN 60, PTS [1st ed. SN i 38; PTS [2nd ed. SN i 85) 6. The Chapter on Aging (*Jarāvagga*)
The Poet Sutta:
“What is the source of verses,
and what is their manifestation?
“Upon what is a verse dependent?
What is the foundation of verses?
“Metre is the source of verses;”
“Letters are their manifestation;
verses are dependent on names;
the poet is the source of verses.”
The sixth chapter is the Chapter on Old Age.
Its summary verse:
Old age, the absence of old age, and a friend.
The Vatthu, the Three Persons,
the Uppatha, and the Dutiya—
this is the chapter completed by the poet.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.61 (SN 1.61, SN 61, PTS [1st ed. SN i 39, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 86) 7. Addhavagga Nāmasutta “Bhikkhus, there are these four names. What four? The name ‘form,’ the name ‘feeling,’ the name ‘perception,’ and the name ‘volitional formations. These, bhikkhus, are the four names.”
“What has overcome everything?
What is it that exists no more?
Of what single thing, indeed, is there no more?”
“All have come under its control.
“Name has overcome everything;
nothing exists beyond name.”
“All have come under the sway of this one thing: name.
—Saṁyutta Nikāya 1.62 (SN 1.62, SN 62, PTS [1st ed. SN i 39; PTS [2nd ed. SN i 87)
7. Addhavagga Cittasutta “By what, indeed, is the world led? ... [The rest of the verse] ...”
By what is one dragged about?
By what single thing is everyone brought under its control?
“The world is led by the mind;
by the mind it is drawn along.
Of this single dharma that is the mind—”
"All have come under its control.
—Saṁyutta Nikāya 1.63 (SN 1.63, SN 63, PTS [1st ed. SN i 39, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 87) 7. Addhavagga (The Chapter on the Course)
The Discourse on Craving:
“By what is the world led?
By what is it dragged along?”
“Kiss, then, is that single thing by which all these beings have been brought under its control?
“The world is led by craving.”
One is dragged about by craving;
by this single thing, craving,
everyone has been brought under its power.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.64 (SN 1.64, SN 64, PTS [1st ed. SN i 39, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 88) 7. Addhavagga The Discourse on Fetters (Saṃyojanasutta) “Bhikkhus, there are these five lower fetters. What five? They are: identity view, doubt, adherence to rules and observances, sensual lust, and ill will.
These, bhikkhus, are the five lower fetters.”
“What is the fetter of the world?
What is its investigation? By the abandoning of what, indeed, [is one liberated]?”
“Nibbāna,” it is said.
“The world is bound by delight,
through the investigation of thought.”
“By the complete abandoning of craving, it is called Nibbāna.
—Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.65 (SN 1.65, SN 65, PTS [1st ed. SN i 39; PTS [2nd ed. SN i 89)
7. The Subsection on Speed (Addhavagga) The Discourse on Bondage (Bandhanasutta) “What binds the world? What is its bond?”
What is his reflection?
And by the relinquishing of what does he cut through every bond?
“The world is bound by delight,
through the investigation of thought;
by the complete abandoning of craving, [it is liberated].”
It cuts through every bond.
—Saṁyutta Nikāya 1.66 (SN 1.66, SN 66, PTS [1st ed. SN i 40; PTS [2nd ed.
SN i 89) 7. Addhavagga
Attahatasutta:
“By what is the world struck down?
By what is it enveloped? By what does it not shine?”
“By what arrow pierced,
and by what is the world always scorched?
“The world is struck down by death,” [he replied].
Enveloped by old age,
pierced by the arrow of craving,
one is perpetually scorched by desire.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.67 (SN 1.67, SN 67, PTS [1st ed. SN i 40, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 90) 7. Addhavagga Uḍḍitasutta “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is suspended, he should not give full admission, he should not give dependence, he should not have a novice attend him, he should not be the leader of a procession, he should not be the leader of a group, he should not be the leader of a caravan, he should not be the leader of a guild, he should not be the leader of a village, he should not be the leader of a town, he should not be the leader of a district. When a bhikkhu is suspended, these ten things do not apply to him.”
“By what is the world raised up?
By what is it surrounded?
By what is the world shut in?”
“Upon what is the world established?
“The world is lifted up by craving and enveloped by old age.”
“The world is hemmed in by death;
the world is established upon suffering.
— *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 1.68 (SN 1.68, SN 68, PTS [1st ed. SN i 40, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 91)
7. The Subsection on Speed (Addhavagga):
The Discourse on Obstructed (Pihitasutta) “By what is the world obstructed?”
Upon what is the world established?
By what is the world raised up?
And by what is it surrounded?”
“The world is hemmed in by death;
the world is established upon suffering;
the world is swept away by craving.”
“Enveloped by old age.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 1.69 (SN 1.69, SN 69, PTS [1st ed. SN i 40, PTS [2nd ed.
SN i 91) 7. Addhavagga
The Discourse on Desire:
“By what is the world bound?
By the removal of what is one liberated?”
“By abandoning desire,
one cuts all bonds.
“The world is bound by longing;”
One is liberated through the discipline of desire;
by the complete abandoning of desire,
one cuts all bonds.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 1.70 (SN 1.70, SN 70, PTS [1st ed. SN i 41, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 92) 7. Addhavagga Lokasutta – The World “Bhikkhus, this world is led by mind, drawn along by mind, and has mind as its master. If one speaks or acts with a defiled mind, suffering follows even as the wheel follows the hoof of the ox that draws the cart. Bhikkhus, this world is led by mind, drawn along by mind, and has mind as its master. If one speaks or acts with a pure mind, happiness follows like a shadow that never departs.”
“In what has the world arisen?
With what does it form intimacy?
By clinging to what does the world exist?”
“In what does the world become distressed?
“The world has arisen in six [spheres];
it forms intimacies with six.”
“It is precisely by clinging to these six that the world is tormented.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, the Chapter on the Six.
Its summary verse:
Name, consciousness, and craving,
fetters, and bonds.
"Overwhelmed by pride and conceited, you desire ten things from the world.
— *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 1.71 (SN 1.71, SN 71, PTS [1st ed. SN i 41; PTS [2nd ed. SN i 93)
8. The Chapter on Cutting (Chetvāvagga). Discourse on Having Cut (Chetvāsutta).
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Standing to one side, that deity addressed the Blessed One in verse:
“What must one cut off to sleep in peace?
What must one cut off to not grieve?”
“O Gotama, what single thing do you approve as the destruction of that one thing?
“Having cut off anger, one sleeps in peace.”
Having cut off anger, one does not grieve;
for anger, O deity, has poison for its root and sweetness for its tip.
“The Noble Ones praise destruction;
for having cut that off, one does not grieve.
— *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 1.72 (SN 1.72, SN 72, PTS [1st ed. SN i 41, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 93)

8. The Chapter on Cutting Off (Chetvāvagga): The Discourse on the Chariot (Rathasutta) “What is the distinguishing mark of a chariot? What is the distinguishing mark of a woman? What is the distinguishing mark of a field? And what is the distinguishing mark of a river?”
What is the mark of a fire?
What is the mark of a kingdom?
And what is the mark of a woman?”
“The banner is the sign of the chariot;
smoke is the sign of the fire;
the king is the sign of the kingdom.”
“The husband is the recognition of a woman. Saṁyutta Nikāya 1.73 (Chetvāvagga)
The Discourse on Wealth:
“What here is the wealth that is best for a person?
What is it that, when well-practiced, brings happiness?”
“What is the sweetest of all tastes?
How does one live whom they call the best of those who live?
“Faith is the greatest wealth for a person in this world.”
The Dhamma well-practiced brings happiness;
truth indeed is the sweetest of flavors;
they say that life lived with wisdom is the best of lives.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.74 (SN 1.74, SN 74, PTS [1st ed. SN i 42, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 95) 8. Chetvāvagga Vuṭṭhisutta (The Rain) “Bhikkhus, just as, when rain pours down in thick droplets on a mountain top, the water flows down following the slope; so too, bhikkhus, for a noble disciple who has abandoned the five lower fetters, there is no returning to this world, but he goes from lightness to lightness, passing away with the breakup of the body to the company of the devas of streaming radiance. Just as, when rain pours down in thick droplets on a mountain peak, the water flows down following the slope; so too, bhikkhus, for a noble disciple who has abandoned the five lower fetters and attenuated lust, hatred, and delusion, there is no returning to this world, but he goes from lightness to lightness, passing away with the breakup of the body to the company of the devas of refulgent glory. Just as, when rain pours down in thick droplets on a mountain peak, the water flows down following the slope; so too, bhikkhus, for a noble disciple who has abandoned the five lower fetters and attenuated lust, hatred, and delusion, there is no returning to this world, but he goes from lightness to lightness, passing away with the breakup of the body to the company of the devas of great fruit. Just as, when rain pours down in thick droplets on a mountain peak, the water flows down following the slope; so too, bhikkhus, for a noble disciple who has abandoned the five lower fetters and attenuated lust, hatred, and delusion, there is no returning to this world, but he goes from lightness to lightness, passing away with the breakup of the body to the company of the devas of the base of infinite space. Just as, when rain pours down in thick droplets on a mountain peak, the water flows down following the slope; so too, bhikkhus, for a noble disciple who has abandoned the five lower fetters and attenuated lust, hatred, and delusion, there is no returning to this world, but he goes from lightness to lightness, passing away with the breakup of the body to the company of the devas of the base of infinite consciousness. Just as, when rain pours down in thick droplets on a mountain peak, the water flows down following the slope; so too, bhikkhus, for a noble disciple who has abandoned the five lower fetters and attenuated lust, hatred, and delusion, there is no returning to this world, but he goes from lightness to lightness, passing away with the breakup of the body to the company of the devas of the base of nothingness. Just as, when rain pours down in thick droplets on a mountain peak, the water flows down following the slope; so too, bhikkhus, for a noble disciple who has abandoned the five lower fetters and attenuated lust, hatred, and delusion, there is no returning to this world, but he goes from lightness to lightness, passing away with the breakup of the body to the company of the devas of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.”
“What is best among those that fly up?
What is most excellent among those that settle down?
What is best among those that go forth?”
“What is best among those who speak?
“The seed is best among things that spring up;
rain is best among things that fall down.”
“Cows are the best among those that go forth;
a son is the best among those who speak.
“Clear knowledge is the best among those things that fly up.”
Ignorance is the worst for those falling [into rebirth];
the Saṅgha is the best among those going forth;
the Buddha is the best among those speaking.”

Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.75 (SN 1.75, SN 75, PTS [1st ed. SN i 42, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 95) 8. Chetvāvagga Bhītāsutta “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is afraid of what is not fearful and not afraid of what is fearful; the person who is not afraid of what is not fearful but is afraid of what is fearful; the person who is afraid of what is not fearful and also afraid of what is fearful; and the person who is neither afraid of what is not fearful nor afraid of what is fearful. And how, monks, is one a person who is afraid of what is not fearful and not afraid of what is fearful? Here, monks, a certain person is afraid of the unwholesome and does not fear the wholesome. This, monks, is called a person who is afraid of what is not fearful and not afraid of what is fearful. And how, monks, is one a person who is not afraid of what is not fearful but is afraid of what is fearful? Here, monks, a certain person is not afraid of the unwholesome and fears the wholesome. This, monks, is called a person who is not afraid of what is not fearful but is afraid of what is fearful. And how, monks, is one a person who is afraid of what is not fearful and also afraid of what is fearful? Here, monks, a certain person is afraid of the unwholesome and also fears the wholesome. This, monks, is called a person who is afraid of what is not fearful and also afraid of what is fearful. And how, monks, is one a person who is neither afraid of what is not fearful nor afraid of what is fearful? Here, monks, a certain person is not afraid of the unwholesome and does not fear the wholesome. This, monks, is called a person who is neither afraid of what is not fearful nor afraid of what is fearful. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
“What is it that causes these many people here to be afraid?
You have proclaimed many paths.
I ask you, Gotama of vast wisdom:”
“Established in what does one not fear the next world?
“Having rightly directed speech and mind,
and committing no evil deeds with the body;”
Living in a home with abundant food and drink,
being faithful, gentle, generous, and kind-spoken—
one who stands firm in these four qualities.
“Established in the Dhamma, one need not fear the world beyond.
— Saṁyutta Nikāya 1.76 (Chetvāvagga)
The Sutta on Not Decaying:
“What decays and what does not decay?
What is said to be the wrong path?”
What is the obstacle to wholesome qualities?
What is the exhaustion of nights and days?
What is the stain of the holy life?
What is the bath that requires no water?
How many fissures are there in the world where wealth does not remain?
“Having come to question the Blessed One,
how shall we understand that?
“The form of mortals decays;”
Name and clan do not decay;
passion is called the wrong path.
Greed is an obstacle to wholesome states.
Time is the wasting away of nights and days;
woman is the stain of the holy life,
wherein this generation becomes entangled.
Austerity and the holy life—
this is the bath where water is the mind.
There are six openings in the world.
Where wealth does not remain:
laziness, negligence,
lack of exertion, and lack of self-restraint.
“Sleep and sloth are the two openings;
one should avoid them entirely.
— *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 1.77 (SN 1.77, SN 77, PTS [1st ed. SN i 43, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 98)

8. The Chapter on Severing (Chetvāvagga) The Discourse on Sovereignty (Issariyasutta) “What is sovereignty in the world? What is the supreme wealth? What is the sweetest of tastes? And what is called the highest happiness?”
What is the supreme among treasures?
What is the weapon that stains the world?
What is the thorn in the world?
What is it that people ward off when it is being taken away?
And what is it that is dear to one who takes it away?
What is it that people do not like when it returns again and again?
“The wise take delight [in this]:
‘In this world, a husband is sovereignty;
a woman is the supreme treasure.’”
Anger is the sword’s edge in the world;
thieves are the floods in the world.
They ward off the thief who is plundering.
“A monk who takes away [defilements] is dear;
the wise rejoice in a monk who returns again and again.”

Saṁyutta Nikāya 1.78 (SN 1.78, SN 78, PTS [1st ed. SN i 44, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 99) 8. Chetvāvagga Kāmasutta “Bhikkhus, having cut off desire for sensual pleasures, having removed the fever of longing, those who have abandoned craving do not come back again to this world.”
“What does one who desires his own welfare not give?
What should a mortal not relinquish?
And what, indeed, should one release for the sake of the wholesome?”
One should not give oneself away, nor should one abandon oneself, lest one be released from evil.
[The Blessed One said: “A person should not give himself away, nor should he sacrifice himself;”
"One should utter speech that is auspicious, and one should not utter what is evil."—Saṁyutta Nikāya 1.79 (SN 1.79, SN 79, PTS [1st ed. SN i 44; PTS [2nd ed. SN i 100)

8. The Chapter on Cutting (Chetvāvagga): The Discourse on Provisions for the Journey (Pātheyyasutta) “What binds one’s provisions for the journey? What is the burden that is difficult to carry? What is the most excellent of goods? And what is the best of all acquisitions?”
What is the abode of enjoyments?
What drags a person along?
And what in this world is difficult to abandon?
“Many beings are bound by something,
like a bird by a snare.
“Faith binds one’s provisions for the journey;”
Glory is the abode of enjoyments;
desire drags a man away.
Desire is difficult to abandon in this world.
“Many beings are bound by desire,
like a bird caught in a snare. (Saṁyutta Nikāya 1.80)

8. The Chapter on Cutting (Chetvāvagga): The Lamp Sutta (Pajjotasutta) “What is the lamp in the world? What is the treasure in the world? What is the best of those who have gone forth? And what is the highest state?”
Who is the one awake in the world?
Who among living beings is active in their work?
And what is their mode of conduct?
What is it that nourishes both the lazy and the diligent,
just as a mother nourishes her son?
What beings depend upon for their livelihood?
“Whatever living beings dwell upon the earth.
“Wisdom is the lamp in the world;
mindfulness is the watchman in the world.”
Cattle are for the livelihood of living beings;
a cool posture is for the cold.
Rain is for both the lazy and the diligent.
She nourishes him as a mother her son;
all beings who depend upon the earth live by the rain.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.81 (SN 1.81, SN 81, PTS [1st ed. SN i 44, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 102) 8. The Chapter on Cutting Off (Chetvāvagga) The Discourse on Being Without Conflict (Araṇasutta) “Monks, there are these three kinds of persons found existing in the world. What three? The person who is without conflict, the person who has cut off conflict, and the person who has transcended conflict. And how, monks, is one a person without conflict? Here, monks, a certain person does not harbor thoughts of enmity toward those who harbor thoughts of enmity; he does not harbor thoughts of ill will toward those who harbor thoughts of ill will; he does not harbor thoughts of cruelty toward those who harbor thoughts of cruelty. He dwells with a mind free from enmity, free from ill will, free from cruelty, vast, exalted, measureless, well-developed. This, monks, is called a person without conflict. And how, monks, is one a person who has cut off conflict? Here, monks, a certain person harbors thoughts of enmity toward those who harbor thoughts of enmity, but he cuts them off; he harbors thoughts of ill will toward those who harbor thoughts of ill will, but he cuts them off; he harbors thoughts of cruelty toward those who harbor thoughts of cruelty, but he cuts them off. This, monks, is called a person who has cut off conflict. And how, monks, is one a person who has transcended conflict? Here, monks, a certain person understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. This, monks, is called a person who has transcended conflict. These, monks, are the three kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
Who in this world are free from conflict?
Whose dwelling does not perish?
Who here fully understand desire?
Whoever is always devoted to service—
whom do they serve? Who is it that, once established in virtue, their mother, father, and brothers honor?
“Who here, though lowly by birth,
do the kṣatriyas pay homage to?
“The world-renunciant who is free from enmity in this world.”
The life lived by recluses does not perish;
recluses thoroughly understand their desires,
for recluses always possess mastery.
Mother, father, and brother honor that ascetic who is firmly established; here,
they do not honor an ascetic who is low-born.
“The nobles pay homage.
This is the eighth chapter, the Chapter on Cutting.
Its summary (uddāna) is as follows:
Having cut through both the chariot and the mind,
one who fears the rain does not decay; having [abandoned] lordship,
sensual pleasure, and provisions for the journey—
And "a lamp from a fire-drill.
The *Devatāsaṃyutta* is complete.
